query: Tungsten is considered for fusion first-wall and divertor service, but it has low strength, limited thermal-shock resistance, a high ductile-brittle transition temperature, and develops dislocation loops and He bubbles under energetic-particle exposure that increase hardening and brittleness; subsequent annealing does not fully remove the damage. Earlier efforts based on cold rolling, wire drawing, and severe plastic deformation sought to improve W, yet fracture resistance remains unresolved and nanocrystalline W still suffers severe damage. Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 showed better radiation resistance than nanocrystalline W and negligible hardening, but Cr-V-rich precipitates appeared at 8 dpa. W29Ta42Cr5V16Hf8 showed neither dislocation loops nor precipitates at 10 dpa, while its greater number of constituents complicates bulk fabrication; the low melting point of Cr also impairs fabrication feasibility in both compositions. For nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 exposed to energetic particles near 8 dpa, what single intervention could suppress precipitate formation while preserving low hardening, radiation resistance, and practical bulk manufacturability? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predict measurable outcomes against the unmodified baseline, define dose and specimen-temperature limits, identify supporting observations from the prior work summarized above, and specify a controlled exposure and post-exposure characterization experiment whose results would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a trace amount of boron (~0.5 at%) into the nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy will suppress the thermodynamically driven Cr–V precipitate nucleation that normally appears at ~8 dpa, while preserving the alloy’s low irradiation hardening, overall radiation resistance, and ease of bulk processing.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 deposited by magnetron sputtering in which irradiation at room temperature or 1073 K to about 8 dpa produces ~3–5 nm Cr–V rich precipitates with a density of ~0.03 nm⁻² and negligible irradiation hardening.
generation.intervention: Incorporate ~0.5 atomic percent boron during alloy synthesis (via powder mixing or sputter target alloying) so that boron preferentially segregates to grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Energetic particle irradiation conditions leading to an accumulated dose near 8 dpa at temperatures from room temperature up to approximately 1073 K.
generation.structural_mediator: Modified grain boundary chemistry and interfacial complexion due to boron segregation.
generation.mechanism: Boron, even in low concentration, has a strong tendency to segregate at grain boundaries. Its presence lowers local grain boundary energies and retards the diffusion and clustering of Cr and V atoms. This kinetic slowdown in solute segregation hinders the nucleation of Cr–V rich precipitates, while maintaining the favorable defect recombination dynamics (and thus low irradiation hardening) inherent to the original alloy. In addition, because the boron content is very low, the overall BCC solid solution and bulk manufacturability remain essentially unaltered.
generation.predicted_outcome: After irradiation to around 8 dpa, the boron-doped alloy will show significantly reduced or eliminated Cr–V precipitate formation (i.e. fewer and/or smaller precipitates as seen by TEM/APT), while nanoindentation hardness remains similar to or within 10% of the undoped alloy’s value. The single-phase BCC structure will be retained and bulk processing routes (such as magnetron sputtering or powder metallurgy followed by spark plasma sintering) will not be adversely affected.
generation.baseline: The unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibits the formation of ~3–5 nm Cr–V rich precipitates at ~8 dpa (density of ~0.03 nm⁻²) with negligible irradiation hardening; however, the precipitates signal a thermodynamic drive toward phase segregation that might compromise long-term ductility or toughness.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to hold for irradiation conditions near 8 dpa and for specimen temperatures between room temperature and ~1073 K. The influence of boron at significantly lower/higher doses or extreme temperatures is less certain and would require further investigation.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends findings from the baseline work (e.g., PMC6397024 conclusions and APT analysis) by combining ideas of grain boundary segregation control drawn from microalloying strategies (well known in steels and other refractory systems) with the unique defect dynamics in HEAs. However, the specific impact of trace boron on grain boundary complexion in W-based HEAs under irradiation is not directly evidenced in the prior work and remains to be demonstrated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 samples—one as a control and one with a ~0.5 at% boron addition during synthesis. Subject both sets to identical energetic particle irradiation at room temperature and 1073 K to a dose of approximately 8 dpa. Post-irradiation, use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atom probe tomography (APT) to quantify precipitate density, size, and distribution. Use nanoindentation to measure hardness and X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase analyses.
measurements: TEM imaging for precipitate morphology and density
APT for grain boundary chemistry and compositional segregation profiles
XRD for phase verification and lattice parameter shifts
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples do not show a statistically significant reduction (at least 50% decrease) in Cr–V precipitate density compared to the undoped baseline, or if the nanoindentation hardness of the boron-doped samples increases by more than 10% (indicating adverse hardening), or if undesired secondary phases are detected that compromise bulk manufacturability, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: APT was performed on a sample irradiated at 1050 K to ~8 dpa using 3-MeV Cu+. After irradiation, we observed no compositional layering of any element (Fig. 5, A to H). Although elemental segregation at grain boundaries is still observed, the precipitation of Cr-rich phases in the grain matrices occurred, as shown in the top-down view of an APT reconstruction with a 25 atomic % (at %) Cr isocomposition surface (Fig. 5, M and N). We have also analyzed the compositional partitioning between the precipitate and the grain matrix (Fig. 5O), showing the enrichment of Cr and V and the depletion of W and Ta inside the black spots. These precipitates are of ~3 to 5 nm in size and show a density of ~0.03 nm−2, both of which are consistent with the in situ–irradiated 8-dpa sample (similar size and density). Therefore, we can conclude that the black spots observed in the irradiated HEA samples at high temperature are Cr- and V-rich precipitates and not irradiation-created dislocation loops.

The present work shows the development of a new class of a refractory HEA based on four elements: 38% W, 36% Ta, 15% Cr, and 11% V in atomic percentages measured by both EDS and APT. Samples were grown using a magnetron sputtering deposition system from pure metal targets and characterized before and after irradiation. Microstructures present a single-phase BCC crystalline structure. The films show a bimodal grain size distribution with ~70% of the grains with sizes in the nanocrystalline regime (≤100 nm) and some regions of ultrafine grain sizes (100 to 500 nm). Concurrent TEM and APT analyses demonstrate the existence of a second phase rich in Cr and V, first forming lamella-like regions to transform to quasi-spherical precipitates after irradiation. Irradiations were carried out both in situ and ex situ at room temperature and 1073 K up to 8 dpa. A thorough analysis of the microstructure shows no sign of radiation-induced dislocation loops, confirming that the observed black spots are indeed second-phase particles.
